question: Can Kolmogorov-Arnold networks learn dynamical models whose governing functions are not sparse in a conventional symbolic library while preserving chaotic invariant behavior?

key_findings.claim: A small spline-based KAN reproduces the Ikeda map's attractor statistics despite rapid trajectory divergence.
key_findings.evidence: A [2,4,2] KAN trained on 10,000 points with an 80/20 split produces Lyapunov exponents [0.5075,-0.7182], near the true [0.5025,-0.7263], while free-running time series separate after a few chaotic iterations.

key_findings.claim: The learned model is non-unique under behavioral validation.
key_findings.evidence: Changing the architecture from [2,4,2] to [2,10,2] yields different learned functions but essentially the same attractor and Lyapunov spectrum; the paper frames this as finite-time shadowing rather than recovery of a unique law.

key_findings.claim: The approach also fits a three-variable chaotic food-chain system that violates a finite polynomial sparsity assumption.
key_findings.evidence: A [3,3] KAN trained on 10,000 samples reproduces the ecosystem attractor, power spectrum, correlation dimension, distance divergences, and Lyapunov exponents reported in the supplement.

key_findings.claim: The paper demonstrates a behavioral surrogate, not discovery of an explicit or identifiable governing equation.
key_findings.evidence: Each edge function remains a fitted cubic spline with many internal parameters, and many architectures can match invariants only inside the observed phase-space domain. No symbolic recovery score or out-of-domain intervention test is reported.

method.core_idea: Replace sparse library regression with sums and compositions of learned univariate splines.
method.mechanism: Train a KAN on one-step state transitions or velocities, then free-run it and compare attractor geometry and dynamical invariants rather than demanding trajectory agreement in a chaotic system.
assumptions: Observed states cover the dynamically relevant domain
One-step fit plus invariant agreement is sufficient for the intended model notion
Spline edge functions remain stable under iteration
Noise and partial observability are negligible

techniques.role: Represents a multivariate flow or map through learned univariate edge functions.
Evaluates attractors, Lyapunov exponents, spectra, and dimensions after trajectories diverge.
Treats a learned orbit as approximating some true orbit rather than the same initial-condition orbit.

evaluations.setting: Ikeda map, 10,000 states, two KAN architectures
evaluations.metric: one-step loss, attractor overlap, Lyapunov exponents
evaluations.result: both architectures reproduce the attractor and exponents near [0.5025,-0.7263]
evaluations.baseline: ground-truth map; sparse methods are asserted to require an infinite expansion but are not quantitatively run

evaluations.metric: attractor, Lyapunov spectrum, power spectrum, correlation dimension, divergence measures
evaluations.result: reported close agreement with ground truth

limitations: Only two noiseless simulated systems are evaluated.
Sparse-regression failure is argued analytically rather than shown under tuned finite libraries.
Spline functions are not converted into compact scientific equations.
Invariant matching within one attractor does not identify counterfactual or out-of-domain dynamics.
failure_modes: Sparse observations permit a spline surrogate with wrong dynamics between samples.
Small one-step error compounds into a spurious attractor.
Noise destabilizes derivatives and fine spline grids.
A behaviorally equivalent model gives incorrect responses under perturbations.
reusable_insights: Validate chaotic surrogates with invariant distributions, not only pointwise rollouts.
Separate behavioral equivalence from equation identification.
Use architecture variation as an identifiability stress test.
open_questions: Can symbolic simplification recover human-readable functions with quantified error?
How stable are invariants under noisy, partial, or off-attractor data?
Which interventions distinguish behaviorally equivalent learned models?

competitive_landscape.title: Discovering governing equations from data: Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamical systems
competitive_landscape.difference: SINDy identifies a sparse explicit equation in a user-specified library; this paper learns nonparametric spline compositions when no short library expansion exists.

competitive_landscape.title: KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: The original KAN paper introduces learnable spline edges and scientific fitting examples; this work specializes them to free-running chaotic maps and flows with invariant-based validation.

competitive_landscape.title: KANDy: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks and Dynamical System Discovery
competitive_landscape.difference: KANDy combines a zero-depth wide KAN with sparse regression to recover explicit governing equations and extends evaluation to PDEs; the reviewed paper emphasizes behaviorally equivalent spline models of two chaotic systems.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: KANs enable general data-driven model discovery beyond sparse governing equations.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Two simulated non-sparse chaotic systems are reproduced by free-running KAN surrogates under several invariant metrics.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The contribution is an early KAN application and a useful non-uniqueness framing, but 'model discovery' means attractor-preserving approximation here, not identifiable symbolic-law recovery.

reviewer_notes: Read all six extracted pages and checked the primary records for SINDy, KAN, and KANDy. Claims about identifiability are reviewer inference from the spline parameterization, domain restriction, and the authors' own non-uniqueness construction.
